attempts.response: Both delays double because the bits have twice as far to travel. I think transmission means the time it takes the packet to get across the cable.

Transmission delay doubles because a longer cable means the transmitter needs twice as long to put the packet onto the cable. Propagation delay also doubles because the signal travels twice the distance at the same speed.

For link A, transmission delay is 1 ms and propagation delay is 1 ms. For link B, transmission delay is 3 ms and propagation delay is 3 ms. I think the longer cable makes transmission take longer too because the packet must travel farther.

Transmission delay is packet size divided by link rate. 1,000 bytes is 8,000 bits, so 8,000 / 8,000,000 = 0.001 s = 1 ms. For 2,000 bytes it is 2 ms. Propagation delay is 600,000 / 200,000,000 = 0.003 s = 3 ms for both packets. Only transmission delay changes because the packet has twice as many bits; distance and propagation speed are unchanged.

Transmission delay is L/R. The 3,000-byte packet has 24,000 bits, so 24,000 / 12,000,000 = 0.002 seconds = 2 ms on both links. Propagation delay is distance/speed: 100,000 / 200,000,000 = 0.0005 s = 0.5 ms for 100 km, and 400,000 / 200,000,000 = 0.002 s = 2 ms for 400 km. Distance changes propagation delay only; packet size and bit rate stay fixed, so transmission delay is unchanged.
